children.html: Gratitude and loneliness in daily life across the adult lifespan
Accepted: 4 November 2021 / Published online: 12 November 2021 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2021

This study examined the association between gratitude and loneliness across the adult lifespan using a seven-day daily diary study design. The sample consisted of young, middle-aged, and older adults (N=128; age M=56.7 years; SD=18.7 years; range=24.2–90.2 years; 46% women). A signifcant Age× Gender× Gratitude interaction efect on loneliness indicated that gratitude and loneliness were negatively associated in general. Results of simple slopes analyses showed that gender diferences in loneliness were signifcant in young adults who were more grateful and in older adults who were less grateful. Women were less lonely than men, on average, and the gender diference was signifcant for those younger and more grateful, or older and less grateful. Thus, the benefcial efect of gratitude on loneliness difered across age and gender. These fndings suggest that the potential benefts of gratitude on social relationships and emotional well-being, such as loneliness, should be examined diferentially for men and women and in the context of changing social relationships in the aging process.
Keywords Gratitude · Loneliness · Emotional well-being · Social relationships · Aging

The positive association between satisfying social relationships and emotional well-being is well-documented (Berkman et al., 2000; Cohen, 2004; Rook & Charles, 2017). Indeed, Lazarus (2006) suggested that emotions can best be understood in the context of social relationships and research on loneliness has documented that lonely individuals are frequently also socially isolated (Cacioppo et al., 2014). Findings have shown that loneliness, the feeling of being disconnected from others, is generally associated with poorer physical and emotional well-being, and unhealthy lifestyles (Cacioppo et al., 2010; Queen et al., 2014; Richard et al., 2017). Studies have sought to identify psychological resources and intervention strategies that may reduce loneliness and the associated negative outcomes (Masi et al., 2011). This raises the question whether there are any aspects of social relationships, such as the feeling of gratitude, for example, that can counteract the negative efects of loneliness (Caputo, 2015; Frinking et al., 2020).

The Socioemotional Selectivity Theory (SST) focuses on developmental changes in social goals across the adult lifespan (Carstensen, 2006; Carstensen et al., 1999). Compared to young adults, older adults are aware of their increasingly shorter future and realize that the emotional satisfaction and meaning from interpersonal and close relationships have priority over the possible gain in knowledge in the future. SST posits that social relationships improve with age (Carstensen et al., 1999). As individuals age, they perceive that time and opportunities left in life are increasingly limited and prioritize social connectedness with familiar and close social partners over seeking new social contacts. Thus, emotion well-being is expected to improve across the adult lifespan when individuals have increasingly limited time. Individuals are expected to increasingly seek to pursue satisfaction and meaning in their social contact as they age. At the same time, empirical evidence suggests that social networks shrink with age (Carstensen et al., 1999). Findings from a 10-year longitudinal study (English & Carstensen, 2014), for example, showed that social networks grew smaller across adulthood, primarily due to the reduction in the number of peripheral partners. In contrast, the number of close social partners remained relatively stable. These fndings suggest

Findings have shown that individuals spend increasingly more time alone as they move across the adult lifespan (Baltes et al., 1990; Larson, 1990). However, being alone does not necessarily imply loneliness and individuals may feel lonely in the presence of others (Jylhä & Saarenheimo, 2010). For instance, loneliness shows a U-shaped association with age across the adult lifespan (Pinquart & Sörensen, 2003), indicating that both young and older adults report higher levels of loneliness compared to middle-aged individuals. In a sample of young adults, more lonely individuals did not difer in their time spent alone, their daily activities, and health behaviors, compared to the less lonely counterparts (Hawkley et al., 2003). In a sample of middle-aged and older adults, however, lonely individuals engaged in more daily activities alone than with others, compared to the less lonely (Queen et al., 2014). These fndings suggest that the association between time spent alone and loneliness may differ across the adult lifespan, such that time spent alone may be more strongly associated with loneliness in midlife and later adulthood than in young adulthood. Thus, the examination of aspects of social relationships that can counteract the negative efects of loneliness may provide important insight into age-related changes in emotional well-being.

SST does not specifcally address the role of gratitude in the development of emotion and social relationships. However, recent studies have shown that gratitude is positively associated with satisfying relationships (Bono & Sender, 2018; Grant & Gino, 2010). Although gratitude has been defned diferently by diferent authors, there is consensus that gratitude is the afective state experienced when individuals recognize that something good has happened to them, and that another person is responsible for this beneft (McCullough et al., 2004; Watkins, 2014). Gratitude has been associated with various positive outcomes (Alkozei et al., 2017; Bartlett & Arpin, 2019). In a sample of predominantly young women, gratitude was negatively associated with loneliness (Caputo, 2015). In addition, older adults who received a gratitude intervention showed a decrease in negative afect and an increase in positive afect, life satisfaction, happiness, and resilience (Salces-Cubero et al., 2019). Given these fndings on the association between gratitude and emotional well-being, it seems reasonable to speculate that gratitude may play a role in social relationships and emotional wellbeing as is consistent with SST. For instance, gratitude promotes prosocial behaviors (McCullough & Tsang, 2004)

The empirical evidence for the potential benefts of gratitude for emotional well-being, however, has two important limitations. First, although fndings suggest that gratitude shows both trait- and state-like properties (Wood et al., 2008), most research has focused on gratitude as a trait (for exceptions, see Bartlett & Arpin, 2019; McCullough et al., 2004; Nezlek et al., 2016). Specifcally, gratitude may be distinguished between generalized gratitude and situationinduced gratitude (Reckart, 2017). Adopting a trait approach in the examination of gratitude means that researchers focus on generalized gratitude, the individual diference in the general tendency to recognize and respond with grateful emotion to other people's benevolent behavior. This approach, however, neglects the within-person component of gratitude, the situation-induced gratitude, which refers to the emotional state individuals experience when they receive a beneft from another person's benevolent behavior (Nezlek et al., 2016; Reckart, 2017). The trait-state distinction is the subject of ongoing debate in personality psychology (Saviola et al., 2020; Zuckerman, 1983). A large body of research has documented that most personality variables show both trait and state components to varying degrees and that it is important to examine both components (Braun et al., 2021; Fleeson, 2017; Geiser et al., 2017; Jayawickreme et al., 2021). The focus on trait gratitude in the current literature emphasizes the stable aspects of gratitude and neglects the transient emotional elements of gratitude that may vary from occasion to occasion in response to another person's kind acts (Bartlett & Arpin, 2019; McCullough et al., 2004; Roberts, 2004). We drew from a previous study that examined gratitude as an afect and how gratitude unfolded in daily interpersonal events (McCullough et al., 2004) and sought to examine the ebb and fow of state gratitude and its association with state loneliness in daily life.

Second, the potential benefits of gratitude may differ due to gender diferences (Kashdan et al., 2009) and age-related changes in social relationships (Chopik et al., 2019). Although emerging evidence supports the benefcial associations of gratitude with social relationships and emotional well-being (Cregg & Cheavens, 2021; Ma et al., 2017), potential gender and age diferences in these benefts have been less examined (Chopik et al., 2019). A previous study examined the moderating efects of gender and age in the link between trait gratitude and subjective well-being (Chopik et al., 2019). However, Chopik et al. (2019) limited their study in the examination of trait gratitude and

encouraged future research on state gratitude. In addition, from a developmental perspective, the relative efect of trait vs. state may change with age (Geiser et al., 2017). The current study sought to examine the possibility that men and women across the adult lifespan may diferentially beneft from state gratitude to reduce state loneliness.
The Role of Gender in Loneliness and Gratitude

Previous studies have utilized SST to examine the role of gender in developmental changes in emotion and social relationships (Birditt & Fingerman, 2003; Robertson & Swickert, 2018). For instance, a recent study examined the roles of age, gender, and forgiveness in the emotional content of autobiographical narratives (Robertson & Swickert, 2018). The authors drew directly from the proposition of SST suggesting that emotion regulation changes with age. Based on previous fndings of gender diferences in emotion regulation and emotion expression, the authors also examined the role of gender in the verbal expression of negative afect (Robertson & Swickert, 2018). Although forgiveness has been defned in diferent ways, the authors adopted a widely accepted defnition of forgiveness by Enright (1996). Enright (1996, p. 108) defned forgiveness as the "willingness to abandon one's right to resentment, condemnation, and subtle revenge towards an ofender who acts unjustly, while fostering the undeserved qualities of compassion, generosity, and even love toward him or her." A signifcant Age×Gender×Forgiveness interaction efect partially supported the proposition from SST that age was negatively associated with the use of negative emotion words but only for men who were low in forgiveness. Although forgiveness has not been explicitly discussed in the context of SST, given the defnition of forgiveness that fosters undeserved compassion and generosity toward an ofender, it is reasonable that forgiveness may increase emotional well-being and social connectedness (Robertson & Swickert, 2018). The authors suggested to integrate the fndings on the role of gender and forgiveness in the understanding of the development of emotion and social relationships (Robertson & Swickert, 2018).

The role of gender in the development of emotion and social relationships can be seen in the gender diferences in the size and composition of social networks. For instance, women tend to have larger social networks than men, whereas men tend to rely more on their spouses for their social networks and emotional support (Santini et al., 2016). Data from 11 European countries, however, show that women in general reported being lonelier than men and the gender diference in loneliness was more pronounced in late life (Hansen & Slagsvold, 2015). For gender diferences in gratitude, women tend to be higher in trait gratitude and

derive more benefts from the experience and expression of gratitude than men (Kashdan et al., 2009). Specifcally, in a young adult sample, women reported greater gratitude and associated their experience of receiving gifts with more benefts and fewer costs than men (Kashdan et al., 2009). In addition, in a sample of young (n=214, Mage=20.5 years, 72.4% women) and older adults (n=77, Mage=69.6 years, 61.8% women), a signifcant Age×Gender interaction indicated that older men experienced substantially less pleasure when they received a gift from another man as opposed to from a woman (Kashdan et al., 2009). Findings on the gender diferences in the expression and experience of gratitude suggest that gratitude may be associated with perceptions of vulnerability and weakness, which may threaten men's masculinity and social standing (Kashdan et al., 2009). Thus, it seems reasonable to examine the roles of gender and gratitude with regard to emotional well-being and social relationships.

Although the afective states of gratitude and loneliness arise to a large extent from the social context (Hawkley et al., 2003; Lazarus, 2006), past research has shown the efect of several individual diference variables, such as age, gender, personality, health conditions, marital status, and employment status, on gratitude and loneliness (Chopik et al., 2019; Kuwert et al., 2014; Watkins, 2014). Individuals higher in extraversion and lower in neuroticism reported receiving more social support (Bolger & Zuckerman, 1995; Von Dras & Siegler, 1997). Better physical health and being married are associated with lower loneliness (Kuwert et al., 2014; Luhmann & Hawkley, 2016). In terms of employment status, homemakers, students, and retirees reported feeling more lonely than unemployed individuals (Caputo, 2015). These individual diference variables were included in the current study as control variables (Cohen et al., 2003). These variables were not of interest by themselves, but they were included in the analyses to make sure that efects attributed to the variables of interests (e.g., age, gender, and gratitude) were not due to these individual characteristics.

The purpose of this study was to address a gap in the literature by examining the within-person experience of gratitude and loneliness in adults' daily life. The current study contributes to the literature by presenting fndings from a seven-day diary study on gratitude and loneliness in a gender-balanced sample of community-residing adults. Specifically, we

extend the literature by examining both the between-person diferences and within-person variabilities in daily gratitude and loneliness, and how daily gratitude and loneliness difer based on individual diferences, including age and gender.

Using a daily diary design, the current study sought to replicate and extend fndings from a previous study (Caputo, 2015) that adopted the trait approach and showed that gratitude and loneliness were negatively associated. The current study addressed two questions. First, we examined the association between state gratitude and loneliness, using data from a seven-day diary study with a sample of communityresiding adults. In doing that, the analyses took into account individual characteristics as control variables (i.e., extraversion, neuroticism, depressive symptoms, life satisfaction, subjective health, marital and employment status) which could interfere with the association between gratitude and loneliness. Second, we examined possible age and gender diferences in the association between gratitude and loneliness. Drawing on SST (Carstensen et al., 1999), we expected that gratitude would have a stronger association with loneliness in older adults, compared to middle-aged and young adults. In addition, based on previous fndings on gender diferences in gratitude (Kashdan et al., 2009), we expected that gratitude would have a stronger association with loneliness in women than in men (Kashdan et al., 2009). Following the study on autobiographical narratives that examined the three-way interaction of Age×Gender×Forgiveness on negative emotion (Robertson & Swickert, 2018), we sought to integrate this recent fnding with current perspectives on SST. Specifcally, we examined the following hypotheses:
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesized that gratitude and loneliness would be negatively associated.

Hypothesis 2: We hypothesized that gratitude and loneliness would be diferentially associated across age and gender. Specifcally, we expected that the efect of gratitude on loneliness would be stronger for older adults compared to middle-aged and young adults, and stronger for women than for men.

The sample consisted of 128 community-residing adults (Mage = 56.7 years; SD = 18.7; range = 24.2–90.2 years; 46% women) who participated in a seven-day diary study. Participants were recruited for a follow-up of a larger study conducted six years earlier in which participants had been assessed daily for 30 consecutive days (Diehl & Hay, 2007). The sampling procedure and sample characteristics have been described elsewhere (Chui & Diehl, 2016; Diehl

In the 6-year follow-up, 132 (55% of the original sample) participants were successfully recruited. Four participants were excluded from analyses because they failed to return the baseline questionnaire although they completed the daily diaries. The overall compliance rate was 98%, with 91% participants completing all seven daily diaries, 7% had one diary missing, and 2% had two to four diaries missing. Participants provided an average of 6.9 diaries (SD =0.51 days; range=3–7 days). The fnal sample consisted of 128 individuals (69 men and 59 women) who returned at least six completed diaries. Thus, the present analyses were based on 878 days of data (an average of 6.86 days of data per person).

Most participants identifed as Caucasian (91%; n=116), 9% (n=11) as African American, and 1% (n=1) as American Indian or Alaska Native. The majority of participants were married (58.6%), 21.1% were single, 12.5% were divorced, 7.0% were widowed, and 0.8% were separated. The median annual household income was $55,000 (mean of $59,100). Most participants (85%) had a bachelor's degree or higher. Most participants were employed fulltime (46%), followed by retired (39%), part-time employed (7%), unemployed (5%), and student with employment (2%). Further analyses used the following three employment statuses: (a) employed full-time, (b) unemployed, and (c) other (retired, part-time employed, or students with employment). Participants were sent a baseline questionnaire and paper diaries in the mail. Trained research assistants gave instructions to the participants over the phone, on how to complete the baseline questionnaire and paper diaries. Participants were instructed to frst complete the baseline questionnaire. They then started the daily diaries the next day. Participants received daily reminders via phone, e-mail or text messages, to complete the diaries before they went to bed. To ensure compliance with the protocol, participants used pre-paid envelopes to return the completed baseline questionnaire and each completed diary the next day.

The daily measures of gratitude and loneliness were adopted from the Positive Affect and Negative Affect Schedule (Watson et al., 1988). Using a 5-point scale (1 = very slightly or not at all; 5 = extremely), participants were instructed each day to "Indicate to what extent you had felt this way during the past 24 h." Participants' responses to the items "grateful" and "lonely" were used to represent gratitude and loneliness. Single-item measures of emotion, including loneliness, have been widely used in previous studies (Moldovan, 2017; Office of National Statistics, 2018; Stack, 1998).

The 20-item Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D; Radloff, 1977) was used to measure depressive symptoms at the baseline. Participants rated their depressive symptoms in the last two weeks on a 4-point scale (0 = rarely or none of the time; 3 = most of the time). The possible scores ranged from 0 – 60. Higher scores indicated higher levels of depressive symptoms. The internal consistency of the CES-D was high (Cronbach's α = 0.88).

Life satisfaction was assessed at baseline using a single item with a 6-point scale (1=Extremely unhappy; 6=Extremely happy). Higher scores indicated better life satisfaction. Single-item measures of life satisfaction are frequently used in large-scale panel studies and have shown satisfactory psychometric properties (Campbell et al., 1976; Lucas & Donnellan, 2012).

In the baseline questionnaire, neuroticism and extraversion were assessed using the Neuroticism and Extraversion subscales of the NEO Five-Factor Inventory (McCrae & Costa, 2003). Each subscale consists of 12 items which are rated on a 5-point scale (0=Strongly disagree; 4=Strongly agree). Higher scores indicated higher neuroticism and higher extraversion. The internal consistencies were high (Cronbach's α=0.90 and 0.85, respectively).

Using the unconditional means model, we examined the between- and within-person variability in loneliness. The intra-class correlation (ICC) was 52%, indicating substantial between- and within-person variability. We proceeded with multilevel modeling due to the nested structure of the data.

First, both the random intercept models and random coeffcients models were estimated to examine the functional form of the relationship between gratitude and loneliness. This determined the relative ft of a linear versus a curvilinear model (i.e., linear or quadratic efects) of gratitude on loneliness. The quadratic efect of gratitude could not be computed due to rank defciency. Thus, the quadratic efect of gratitude was dropped from further analyses.

Results showed similar fxed efects in the random intercept models and random coefcients models. After testing the assumptions, the assumption of normality of the level-1 residuals seemed violated. We then proceeded to Bayesian multilevel modeling which does not require any assumptions about the distribution of the data (Finch et al., 2019), using the default set of priors in the MCMCglmm library (Hadfeld, 2010). The Bayesian counterparts of the random intercept models and random slopes models converged. However, the histogram of the distribution of the random efect of slope in the Bayesian random coefcients models showed that the estimate of the random efect of slope did not converge on a single value. This suggested that the random slope should be dropped from the models. We compared the random intercept models and the corresponding Bayesian models. The coefcients in the random intercept models and the posterior means in the corresponding Bayesian models showed essentially identical results. In addition, we compared the 95% confdence intervals and p values with the Bayesian counterparts, 95% credibility intervals and Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) p values. Again, the results were essentially identical. All analyses were performed in R (R Core Team, 2021) using the nlme (Pinheiro et al., 2021), lme4 (Bates et al., 2015), and MCMCglmm (Hadfeld, 2010) libraries. Table 3 presents results of the two nested random intercept models.

To address Hypothesis 1, Model 1 tested the efect of gratitude on loneliness controlling for other variables of interest. The signifcant efect of day showed that loneliness decreased across the seven-day period of assessment, 𝛾10 = -0.02. t(742)=-2.36, p<0.05. Gratitude was negatively associated with loneliness, 𝛾20 = -0.13, t(742)=-4.97, p<0.001. On days when participants experienced more than average gratitude, they reported feeling less lonely. Women reported a lower level of loneliness than men, 𝛾02 = -0.29, t(115)=-2.89, p<0.01, and depressive symptoms were positively associated with loneliness, 𝛾04 = 0.03, t(115)=3.43, p<0.001.

To address Hypothesis 2, interaction efects of age and gender were added in Model 2. Similar to the results of Model 1, the signifcant efect of day in Model 2 showed that loneliness decreased across the period of assessment, 𝛾10 = -0.02. t(742)=-2.46, p<0.05. The efects of gender and gratitude were also signifcant, ps<0.01. However, interpretation of the efects of gender and gratitude needs to be considered in view of the signifcant Age×Gender×Gratitude interaction efect, 𝛾23= 0.01, t(739)=2.34, p<0.05. Figure 1 graphically presents the three-way interaction. For men, gratitude and loneliness showed the same negative association across age. However, for women, the negative association between gratitude and loneliness was signifcantly stronger in younger women than in older women.

Rather than favoring one particular statistical approach, different approaches and a variety of criteria should be used and compared in the decision of the best-ftting model because diferent model selection approaches have diferent strengths and weaknesses (Steele, 2013). Thus, to identify the model for interpreting results in an optimal way, we considered various model selection approaches. First, the AIC and BIC showed that Model 1 provided the better ft. Results of the Likelihood Ratio Test (LRT) also showed that the simpler Model 1 ft signifcantly better than Model 2, χ2 (4)=25.09, p<0.001. Second, we followed up the analyses using bootstrapping confdence intervals (Finch et al., 2019). The 95% confdence intervals (CIs) of the Age×Gender×Gratitude interaction efect were examined using fve bootstrapping methods. With the exception of the basic method that the model failed to converge, results of confdence intervals showed that the Age×Gender×Gratitude interaction efect was signifcant, using the percentile, 95% CI=[0.001, 0.01], norm, 95% CI=[0.001, 0.01], Wald, 95% CI=[0.001, 0.01], and profle methods, 95% CI= [0.001, 0.01]. Third, the results of the Bayesian multilevel modeling showed that the Age×Gender×Gratitude interaction efect was signifcant, 𝛾23 = 0.006, 95% CI=[0.001, 0.01], pMCMC<0.05.

Finally, we examined the simple slopes, regions of significance, and confidence bands of the Age × Gender × Gratitude interaction effect (Preacher et al., 2006). The results of the simple slopes analysis showed that the gender difference in loneliness was significant for younger (-1 SD below grand mean) and more grateful individuals (+ 1 SD within-person mean), simple slope = -0.38, t = 2.50, p < 0.05, and older (+ 1 SD above grand mean) and less grateful individuals (-1 SD withinperson mean), simple slope = -0.38, t = -2.48, p < 0.05. This study examined age and gender diferences in gratitude and loneliness in adults' daily life. Findings supported Hypothesis 1, indicating that greater daily gratitude was, in general, associated with less loneliness. In terms of Hypothesis 2, findings showed that the association

between gratitude and loneliness varied by age and gender. For younger adults, the association between gratitude and loneliness was stronger in women than in men. In contrast, for older adults, the association between gratitude and loneliness was stronger in men than in women. Thus, the gender difference in the beneficial effects of gratitude in older adults was in the opposite direction as we had hypothesized. In partial support to propositions of the Socioemotional Selectivity Theory (Carstensen et al., 1999), age was associated with greater benefts from gratitude. However, this efect was more pronounced for older men compared to older women. We discuss these fndings with reference to the literature on gender diferences in social relationships and aging.

SST does not specifcally address the roles of gratitude and gender with regard to emotional well-being and social relationships. Similar to previous fndings that adopted the trait approach (Caputo, 2015), our fndings showed that state gratitude and state loneliness, as assessed in daily diaries, were negatively associated. For gender diferences in loneliness, our fndings showed that men, in general, reported a higher level of loneliness than women. However, the signifcant Age×Gender×Gratitude interaction indicated that the gender diference in loneliness was dependent on age and level of gratitude. Specifcally, results of simple slopes analyses showed that the gender diferences in young adults who were more grateful, and older adults who were less grateful, were statistically signifcant. We draw on the general heuristic of one scale point on a 10-point scale as the measure of efect size, such that diferences below 1.0 were considered not to reach practical signifcance (Jebb et al., 2020). As shown in Fig. 1, the gender diferences were larger than 0.5 point on the 5-point scale of loneliness in young adults who were more grateful and in older adults who were less grateful. Thus, using this general heuristic, the gender diferences would have reached practical signifcance.

Conficting evidence in gender diferences in loneliness has been reported (Pinquart & Sörensen, 2010). The mixed fndings regarding gender diferences in loneliness may be explained by the fndings from a longitudinal study of older adults in Israel (Iecovich et al., 2011). Loneliness tended to fuctuate more in men than in women across the 18-year study period, suggesting that compared to women, men may be more reactive to the loss of a partner or other close ties, and to declines in health. In contrast, women may be better able to cope with age-related losses because women tend to have larger support networks than men. Thus, our fndings provided support to utilize SST to examine gender diferences in loneliness in view of the changing social
relationships and health status in the aging process (Iecovich et al., 2011).

The mixed fndings in terms of age diferences in loneliness (Luhmann & Hawkley, 2016; Pinquart & Sörensen, 2003), however, may also be explained as a measurement artifact. The UCLA Loneliness Scale (Hughes et al., 2004; Russell, 1996) is the most commonly used measure of trait loneliness. Most items in the scale ask participants how often they feel being isolated or whether they have people to talk to. Only one item asks participants to rate "I do not feel alone." There is no item in the UCLA Loneliness Scale that uses the terms "lonely" or "loneliness" (Goossens et al., 2014). In the present study, however, participants rated the extent to which they "felt lonely" during the past 24 h. It is possible that in a culture that highly values personal independence, individuals may not feel comfortable to admit that they feel lonely, resulting in an under-reporting of feelings of loneliness. Evidence supporting this assumption was provided in a qualitative study of independence in older adults in Canada (Bell & Menec, 2015). In this study, participants talked about the expectation of being independent in old age, the fear of being a burden, and the fear of being perceived as lonely (Bell & Menec, 2015). Participants also talked about the need for resources and supports in the community to cope with social exclusion and staying socially connected (Bell & Menec, 2015). Overall, the terms "lonely" and "loneliness" carry negative connotations (Pinquart & Sörensen, 2003), such that participants may not admit that they feel lonely and the level of loneliness may be underestimated in studies of loneliness and aging.

Consistent with past research (Kashdan et al., 2009), our findings provided support for the differential beneficial efect of gratitude across age. Similar to a previous study that examined the role of forgiveness, an attribute that may increase emotional well-being and social connectedness (Robertson & Swickert, 2018), our fndings of the benefcial efects of gratitude on loneliness was consistent with the SST propositions regarding changing emotional well-being and social networks across the adult lifespan. In the present study, gratitude was more benefcial for younger women than younger men to reduce loneliness. In contrast, gratitude was more benefcial for older men than older women. Our fndings added to the literature of gratitude and examined state gratitude, that is, the situation-induced gratitude that arises from daily social interactions (Nezlek et al., 2016; Reckart, 2017).

A major source for gratitude commonly lies in the giveand-take nature of social relationships (Lazarus, 2006). To feel grateful, the recipient acknowledges that the giver has something of value to give and appraises the giver's action as a self-less or kind act (Lazarus, 2006; Watkins, 2014). Gratitude serves as a moral barometer that motivates prosocial behaviors (McCullough & Tsang, 2004). With increasing age, individuals may become more dependent on others to cope with chronic health conditions and potential disability (Rook et al., 2007), yet may also feel more gratitude for any received assistance. Thus, the benefcial efect of gratitude may be more pronounced in older men than in older women because older men with chronic health conditions are more likely being taken care of by their spouses (Chui et al., 2014). In contrast, compared to young women, it may be harder for young men to express and experience gratitude as recipients of help and kindness, which can threaten their perceptions of masculinity that focus on independence and self-sufciency (Kashdan et al., 2009). For instance, young men who were diagnosed of fbromyalgia experienced a reconstruction of their masculine identity in the difcult transition from a strong and active body to a vulnerable and helpless body (Sallinen et al., 2019). Further studies to examine the roles of gender and trait vs. state gratitude in emotional well-being are needed to more comprehensively understand these issues in the context of SST.

Consistent with past research, loneliness was positively associated with depressive symptoms (Hawkley, 2015). In contrast, we did not fnd any association between loneliness, personality, and marital and employment status as previously reported (Caputo, 2015). Compared to the study by Caputo (2015), our sample consisted of more older adults. It is possible that the associations between loneliness, personality, marital and employment status are more pronounced in younger adults than in older adults. Younger adults who are not married and do not participate in the labor force may have more restricted social networks compared to their agenormative peers and may, therefore, be more prone to experiencing loneliness. This assumption seems justifed because previous research has reported age diferences in loneliness across the adult lifespan (Pinquart & Sörensen, 2003). The possible diferential efects of social networks on loneliness in diferent age groups requires further investigation.

The current study has several limitations. First, our sample was relatively healthy, high functioning, and communitydwelling. Past research has shown that individuals with a more disadvantaged socioeconomic background reported

higher loneliness and lower levels of gratitude (Luhmann & Hawkley, 2016). Therefore, results may not be generalizable to more diverse and less healthy populations. Given the changing racial and ethnic composition of the population and the associations between health inequality, race, and socioeconomic status (Dickman et al., 2017), future studies should use more diverse samples to examine the age diferences in the association between gratitude and emotional well-being in diferent racial and ethnic groups (Boehm et al., 2011).

Second, the present study cannot tease apart any causeand-efect associations between gratitude and loneliness (Alkozei et al., 2017). The afective states of gratitude and loneliness were reported at the same time. A research design with multiple assessments throughout a day would be needed to address the directionality of efects (van der Krieke et al., 2015).

Third, age diferences rather than age-related change were examined in this study. Thus, the efects of cohort and chronological age are confounded (Li & Schmiedek, 2002). That is, we cannot ascertain with certainty whether the age diference in the benefcial efects of gratitude stem from age-related changes or refect possible cohort diferences. Past research reported mixed fndings in age diferences in gratitude and loneliness (Allemand & Hill, 2016; Luhmann & Hawkley, 2016). Future studies should adopt multiple time-scale designs to disentangle the efects of trait vs. state conceptualizations of gratitude and loneliness and the efects of cohort and age (Ram & Diehl, 2015).

Fourth, only extraversion and neuroticism were assessed as personality traits in the present study. The other three dimensions of the Big Five were not examined because this study was part of a larger study on daily stress and emotions. Only extraversion and neuroticism were measured because these two traits have been predominantly associated with daily stress and emotions (Bolger & Zuckerman, 1995; Swickert et al., 2002). Also, previous studies have documented associations between extraversion, neuroticism, and loneliness (Cacioppo et al., 2010; Freund & Baltes, 1998). Future studies may examine the role of the other three dimensions of the Big Five on loneliness and gratitude (Wood et al., 2010).

The ffth limitation is methodological in nature. Most participants started the seven-day diaries on Mondays and a few started on Tuesdays. We acknowledge that the day of the week may afect a person's emotional well-being (Trampe et al., 2015) and that the current study did not control for that beyond holding the start of the diaries mostly constant. Thus, it cannot be ruled out that the fnding of a signifcant efect of day on loneliness may be a result of when a participant started their daily diary rather than day of the week. The study design does not allow us to disentangle these efects.

Sixth, Bayesian multilevel modeling was used in the follow-up analyses to substantiate the results presented. We acknowledge the importance of using informative priors based on prior research (Finch et al., 2019). However, the default set of priors was used in our analyses because there was not sufcient evidence in previous studies to specify the prior distribution for each of the model parameters. With large sample sizes, results using default or informative priors usually show no diference (Finch et al., 2019). Future studies may use a larger sample to further examine the role of gratitude in emotional well-being and social relationships.

Seventh, we acknowledge the potential lack of power in our study. Statistical power in multilevel modeling has been an issue of concern and diferent approaches have been proposed to assess the complex infuences on power in multilevel models (Snijders, 2005). In particular, the power analysis of interaction efects in multilevel models shows that increasing sample sizes enables more power gain than increasing observations holding all other parameters equal (Lane & Hennes, 2017). However, increasing sample sizes comes with a trade-of of reducing predictor variance and, in turn, undermines power (Lane & Hennes, 2017). In addition, the call for the importance of statistical power in psychology research may have created the unintended false impression that a large sample is the best or only remedy for increasing power, without considering alternative design and analysis strategies (McClelland, 2000). In the current study, statistical power was optimized by the qualifying of the dependent variable, that is, adjusting for the control variables (Cohen, 1988). On a related issue, we recognize the limitation of the use of the general heuristic (Jebb et al., 2020) to interpret the efect size of the signifcant Age× Gender× Gratitude interaction efect. Although we recognize the importance of efect size reporting, guidance on efect size measures for multilevel modeling is currently lacking in the literature (Lorah, 2018).

Lastly, in a less than optimal way, but mostly motivated by limiting the response burden on study participants (Shrout & Lane, 2011), single-item measures were used for the key variables of gratitude and loneliness. Singleitem measures of key variables are common in large epidemiological and public health studies (Lucas & Donnellan, 2012; Meng et al., 2014). To our knowledge, no research has examined the psychometric property of the single-item measures of gratitude and loneliness. However, previous studies have provided support for the longitudinal reliability and validity of single-item measures, including measures of happiness, life satisfaction, self-esteem, selfrated physical health, and self-rated mental health (Ahmad et al., 2014; Lucas & Donnellan, 2012; Meng et al., 2014; Moldovan, 2017; Robins et al., 2001). Findings of the present study showed that the association between gratitude and loneliness varied across age and gender. Contrary to our expectation, the association between gratitude and loneliness was stronger in older men, compared to older women. Our fndings speak to the importance of age and gender diferences in the examination of state gratitude and loneliness in the everyday social context. For instance, gratitude interventions have been used to improve emotional well-being in older adults (Bartlett & Arpin, 2019; Salces-Cubero et al., 2019). However, gender diferences in the efect of gratitude interventions have been less examined. Our results are consistent with the proposition from Socioemotional Selectivity Theory that social relationships improve with age (Carstensen et al., 1999) and such improvements may be related to how gratitude is expressed and regulated in these social relationships. Although the role of gratitude is not explicitly discussed in the context of SST, our fndings indicated that assessing gratitude may be fruitful moving forward in the examination of emotional wellbeing and social relationships across the adult lifespan. The fndings help to shed light on the role of gratitude in social relationships across adulthood, which may have particular implications for real-life situations such as caregiving and care-receiving in old age.
